new_statements.quote: 1.2.6. Accent. One additional feature of Pawnee speech is that of accent or stress. This feature does not seem to be phonemic, since there are no examples of it establishing morphemic contrasts. With polysyllabic nouns and particles, stress generally, though not always, falls on the first syllable. With verb forms, however, the placement of stress is more variable. What the conditioning factors for its placement are is not known at this time, and for this reason there will be no attempt at accounting for it.

new_statements.relation_note: Placement agrees with the catalog's initial coding (initial stress, StressTyp2 from this very source) but only as a dominant tendency restricted to polysyllabic nouns and particles: the source says stress is not phonemic, admits exceptions ('though not always'), and says verb-form placement is variable with unknown conditioning. An exceptionless (fixed-strict) initial coding for the word in general is not supported by the source; a fixed-dominant initial with a nouns/particles domain restriction is what it supports. new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-phonemic. In polysyllabic nouns and particles it usually (not always) falls on the first syllable; in verb forms its placement is variable and the conditioning factors are unknown, so the grammar does not account for it. The phonetic examples on p.14 mostly show initial accent in nouns ([pí:tʌ] 'man', [táku] 'someone', [čáhriks] 'person', [páču:kaʔ] 'turnip', [káhcuʔ] 'herb', [kí:cuʔ] 'neck', [kísuc] 'grape') with at least one non-initial noun ([kiwʌ́ku] 'fox').
new_statements.exceptions: 'generally, though not always' for nouns and particles; verb forms 'more variable', conditioning 'not known at this time'; p.14 example [kiwʌ́ku] 'fox' accented on the second syllable; p.16 notes that short-vowel tense/lax variation depends on 'tempo of speaking, stress placement, etc.' and that [ʌ] 'frequently occurs in open syllables, especially when the syllable is stressed'. Text 9.1 (pp.339-342) is in phonemic transcription without accent marks.
new_statements.identity_note: Parks 1976 describes the South Band dialect (p.1: 'There are two major dialect divisions within Pawnee. One of these, called South Band, and the one described in this grammar, was spoken by the three eastern bands.. The Skiri.. constitutes a second dialect.'); the two dialects are 'fully mutually intelligible' and differ 'primarily' phonetically. The catalog item pawn1254 covers both dialects.

audit.recode_to: undetermined (non-phonemic stress, placement variable/conditioning unknown; initial tendency in nouns and particles only) — or, if a position must be kept, fixed-dominant initial with not in the strict set and word-class restriction (nouns/particles), never fixed-strict

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: the Parks 1976 p.17 accent passage is verbatim in the Rosetta scan we hold. But the classification 'fixed-strict' (initial, counts as exceptionless (the strict set), word domain) is not what the held sources say. (a) Parks 1976, the deciding quote itself: stress 'does not seem to be phonemic'; in polysyllabic nouns and particles it 'generally, though not always' falls on the first syllable; in verbs placement is 'more variable' and its conditioning 'is not known' — in a polysynthetic language where verb forms dominate, this supports at most an initial tendency restricted to nouns/particles. StressTyp2 itself coded the pattern with msdomain=nouns and the editor note 'maybe verbs too?'. (b) Parks & Pratt 2008 p.15 (held page image, same author, 32 years later, Skiri dialect): stress not phonemic; recurring tendencies are initial OR peninitial (when V1 short and V2 long) AND antepenult or penult, 'but
